description: Question: why does the world not simply double its harvest by doubling fertiliser? Idea: the yield response curve and the law of diminishing returns. Mitscherlich (1909): each extra kilogram of a limiting nutrient closes a fixed fraction of the remaining gap to the attainable yield, Y = Y0 + A(1 − e^(−cN)), so its marginal product dY/dN = A·c·e^(−cN) falls exponentially. The World Bank (FAO data) gives fertiliser use (kg of N + P₂O₅ + K₂O per hectare of arable land) and cereal yield (kg/ha) for about 220 countries. Polars fits the curve by a grid search over c (a cross join with 150 trial values; for each, A and Y0 by closed-form least squares; a profile-likelihood interval for c), computes each country's marginal product and residual, and the grain each successive 50 kg/ha buys. Aha (data of November 2026, 136 countries in the fit): half of the whole response comes in the first 54 kg/ha (95% profile interval 37–87); the first 50 kg/ha buy about 2,040 kg of grain, 41 kg per kg, the next 200 kg/ha about 2,100 kg, 10.5 kg per kg, and one more kilogram returns 5 kg of grain at about 190 kg/ha and 1 kg at about 310 kg/ha. The curve beats the straight line (R² 0.57 against 0.42). Fifteen countries sit on the flat part (under 3 kg per extra kg): Egypt (598 kg/ha), Viet Nam, Colombia, Bangladesh, Brazil and China (about 390–420) among them; there most of the extra nitrogen leaves as nitrate in rivers and N₂O in the air. Countries' paths since 2000 show the other way out: China cut fertiliser from 481 kg/ha (2016) to 393 (2024) while its cereal yield rose from 6,017 to 6,495 kg/ha. The curve is not one farm's: the United States reaches 8,414 kg/ha on 128 kg/ha (92% above the curve) and India 3,632 on 214 (26% below), the climate, irrigation, seed and crop mix the cross-country curve averages over; and its exponential form forces the slope to zero, so read the flat part as 'little', not 'nothing'. Caveats: across countries the curve carries climate, irrigation, seed and crop mix (a test of irrigation on the residuals is in the study); fertiliser is all three nutrients and only per arable hectare, so 45 countries with under 200,000 ha of arable land or over 800 kg/ha (fertilised pasture and plantations: New Zealand, Ireland, Malaysia, the Gulf) are left out of the fit (shown as crosses); latest years differ; the agronomic N-response is measured per field and crop in rate trials. Next: FAOSTAT's nitrogen-only use and soil nutrient budget (the surplus on the flat part), prices for the economic optimum rate, climate for the curve's ceiling.
name: Fertiliser and diminishing returns
